nodes.title: Statements & Logical Connectives
points: Statement (Proposition): A declarative sentence which is either true or false, but not both simultaneously.
Imperative (commands), interrogative (questions), exclamatory, and open sentences (truth depends on context) are NOT statements.
Truth value: 'T' if statement is true, 'F' if false.
Conjunction (p ∧ q): True only when BOTH p and q are true; otherwise false.
Disjunction (p ∨ q): False only when BOTH p and q are false; otherwise true.
Negation (¬p): Reverses the truth value (¬T = F, ¬F = T).

nodes.title: Conditional & Biconditional Statements
points: Conditional / Implication (p ⇒ q): 'If p then q'. False ONLY when antecedent p is true and consequent q is false (T ⇒ F = F).
Equivalent formulations of p ⇒ q: 'p is sufficient for q', 'q is necessary for p', 'p implies q', 'q follows from p'.
Important equivalence: p ⇒ q ≡ ¬p ∨ q.
Biconditional / Double Implication (p ⇔ q): 'p if and only if q'. True when both p and q have the SAME truth value (T ⇔ T = T and F ⇔ F = T).
Biconditional equivalence: p ⇔ q ≡ (p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p) ≡ (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (¬q ∨ p).

formulas.label: Conditional truth
formulas.expr: T ⇒ F = F (all other cases T)

nodes.title: Converse, Inverse & Contrapositive
points: Given a conditional statement p ⇒ q:
Converse: q ⇒ p (interchange antecedent and consequent).
Inverse: ¬p ⇒ ¬q (negate both antecedent and consequent).
Contrapositive: ¬q ⇒ ¬p (interchange and negate both).
Fundamental Equivalence: A conditional statement is logically equivalent to its contrapositive: (p ⇒ q) ≡ (¬q ⇒ ¬p).
Converse and Inverse are logically equivalent: (q ⇒ p) ≡ (¬p ⇒ ¬q).

nodes.title: Quantifiers & Quantified Statements
points: Universal Quantifier (∀): 'For all' or 'For every'. Statement ∀x ∈ A, P(x) is true if P(x) holds for EVERY element of A.
Existential Quantifier (∃): 'There exists' or 'For some'. Statement ∃x ∈ A such that P(x) is true if P(x) holds for AT LEAST ONE element of A.
Negation of Universal Statement: ¬[∀x ∈ A, P(x)] ≡ ∃x ∈ A such that ¬P(x).
Negation of Existential Statement: ¬[∃x ∈ A such that P(x)] ≡ ∀x ∈ A, ¬P(x).
In negation, change ∀ to ∃, change ∃ to ∀, and negate the condition P(x).

nodes.title: Tautology, Contradiction & Contingency
points: Tautology (t): A compound statement whose truth value is 'T' for all possible truth assignments of its components.
Contradiction / Fallacy (c): A compound statement whose truth value is 'F' for all possible truth assignments.
Contingency: A statement that is neither a tautology nor a contradiction (truth table contains both T and F).
Standard Tautology Examples: p ∨ ¬p ≡ t; p ⇒ p ≡ t; p ⇔ p ≡ t.
Standard Contradiction Examples: p ∧ ¬p ≡ c.

nodes.title: Duals & Negation of Compound Statements
points: Principle of Duality: Two compound statements are duals if one is obtained from the other by replacing ∧ with ∨, ∨ with ∧, t with c, and c with t.
CRITICAL: The negation symbol (¬) is NEVER changed while writing the dual.
De Morgan's Laws: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q.
Negation of Conditional: ¬(p ⇒ q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q (notice it is a conjunction, never an if-then!).
Negation of Biconditional: ¬(p ⇔ q) ≡ (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ (q ∧ ¬p) ≡ (p ⇔ ¬q).

nodes.title: Algebra of Statements (Logical Equivalences)
points: Idempotent Laws: p ∧ p ≡ p; p ∨ p ≡ p.
Commutative Laws: p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p; p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p.
Associative Laws: (p ∧ q) ∧ r ≡ p ∧ (q ∧ r); (p ∨ q) ∨ r ≡ p ∨ (q ∨ r).
Distributive Laws: p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r); p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r).
Identity Laws: p ∧ t ≡ p; p ∨ c ≡ p; p ∧ c ≡ c; p ∨ t ≡ t.
Absorption Laws: p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p; p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p.
Involution (Double Negation): ¬(¬p) ≡ p.

formulas.label: Identity laws
formulas.expr: p ∧ t ≡ p , p ∨ c ≡ p

formulas.label: Absorption laws
formulas.expr: p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p , p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p

nodes.title: Switching Circuits & Boolean Networks
points: Switch S₁ represents statement p; switch S₂ represents q. Closed switch = 1 (T), open switch = 0 (F).
Switches in SERIES: Connected one after another. Current flows only if BOTH are closed ⟹ Represents Conjunction (p ∧ q).
Switches in PARALLEL: Connected across common junctions. Current flows if AT LEAST ONE is closed ⟹ Represents Disjunction (p ∨ q).
Complementary switch S₁' represents ¬p.
Circuit simplification: Use algebra of statements to simplify the symbolic switching expression, reducing the number of switches required.

nodes.title: Must-Know Board Proofs & Truth Tables
points: Board Favourite #1: Prove logical equivalence using truth table: p ⇔ q ≡ (p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p).
Board Favourite #2: Prove that [p ⇒ (q ⇒ r)] ≡ [(p ∧ q) ⇒ r] using truth table.
Board Favourite #3: Write the negation of compound statement step-by-step: (p ∨ q) ⇒ (p ∧ ¬r).
Board Favourite #4: Express switching circuit in symbolic form, simplify using laws of logic, and draw the equivalent simplified circuit.
Board Presentation Rule: When proving equivalence using truth table, explicitly mention: 'Columns X and Y are identical, hence LHS ≡ RHS'.

formulas.label: Truth table columns rule
formulas.expr: Columns X and Y identical ⟹ LHS ≡ RHS

nodes.title: MHT-CET 5-Second Hacks, Negation Traps & Duals
points: Negation Trap: Negation of 'If it rains, then the school is closed' is 'It rains AND the school is NOT closed' (never use 'if-then' in negation!).
Dual Trap: In writing duals, DO NOT change ¬p. Only swap ∧ ↔ ∨ and t ↔ c.
Row Count in Truth Table: A statement with n distinct propositional variables has exactly 2ⁿ rows (e.g., 3 variables p, q, r ⟹ 2³ = 8 rows).
5-Second Tautology Check: If an implication has conclusion t (always true), the statement is automatically a tautology: p ⇒ t ≡ t.
Contrapositive Quick Hack: Contrapositive of p ⇒ (q ∨ r) is ¬(q ∨ r) ⇒ ¬p ≡ (¬q ∧ ¬r) ⇒ ¬p.
